The two edge vectors of the lifted patch are (du, 0, f_x du) and (0, dv, f_y dv), and their cross product is (f_x, f_y, -1) du dv after the two-by-two cofactors are taken. That cross product is perpendicular to the surface because it is perpendicular to both edges, and it points downward, since its third component is negative. Negating it to match the upward orientation gives minus f_x, minus f_y, 1, in the sense that the surface is above its base, and scaling by du dv gives the vector area element. The length of this vector is the square root of 1 plus f_x squared plus f_y squared, which is exactly the scalar area element, so the two differ only in that one carries the direction of the surface. That is the whole reason a flux integral uses the vector form: the dot product with the field needs a direction, and the surface must supply one.

questions.stem: A flat plate lies in the plane 2x plus 3y plus 6z equal to 12, and the coordinate planes cut it into a triangle in the first octant. First report the length of the vector of coefficients of the plane, then report the area of the triangle. Report the area only.

multiplies the three intercepts together as though the region were the box they bound
reports the area of the shadow on the xy-plane instead of the area of the plate

questions.learningObjective: evaluate a scalar surface integral of a coordinate over a triangular plate
questions.stem: A triangular plate has its corners at the points (6, 0, 0), (0, 4, 0) and (0, 0, 3), which lie in the plane 2x plus 3y plus 4z equal to 12. questions.explanation: The mass is the surface integral of x over the plate, and since x is a linear function its average over a triangle equals its value at the centroid, which is the mean of the three vertex values. Those are 6, 0 and 0, so the average is 2. The plate's own area comes from half the length of the cross product of the two edges out of the vertex (6, 0, 0), namely minus 6, 4, 0 and minus 6, 0, 3. Their cross product is 12, 18, 24, whose length is the square root of 144 plus 324 plus 576, that is 6 times the square root of 29, so the area is 3 times the square root of 29. Multiplying the area by the average value 2 gives 6 times the square root of 29, that is 32.3110. Projecting onto the xy-plane instead would give 12 times 2 = 24, which is the first moment of the shadow rather than of the plate.
questions.hint: A linear function averages over a triangle at its centroid, so get the centroid value and the plate's own area.

reports the area of the plate and ignores the field altogether
cancels the three coordinate contributions against each other as though the field were antisymmetric

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Why closed surfaces are the useful case
questions.learningObjective: explain what a closed surface lets a flux integral detect
questions.stem: Explain why flux integrals over closed surfaces are worth computing even though they must be broken up into pieces, and say what the total measures about the field inside.

answer.exemplar: A closed surface has the property that the region it bounds is on one side of it, so an outward normal can be chosen consistently everywhere at once. That consistency is what turns a collection of unrelated patch integrals into a single number with a meaning: because every patch is oriented away from the same interior, any material or field that leaves the interior must cross the surface outward, and anything that enters must cross it inward, so the signed total measures the net amount accumulating inside, positive where the field is a source and negative where it is a sink. A field that goes in through one patch and comes out through another of equal strength gives a total of exactly zero, which is why a field with no sources anywhere is invisible to every closed surface. An open surface has no such reading, since there is no interior for inflow and outflow to balance against, and its flux changes sign under a reversal that carries no physical content.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to carry the inflow and outflow balance, since that cancellation is exactly what the closed-surface total records and the reason zero is meaningful.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to material that leaves the interior, and where else it could have gone.

Adding the two pieces gives 9 pi times the square root of 2 plus 9 pi, which is 9 pi times the quantity square root of 2 plus 1, that is 68.2603. The two pieces are genuinely different surfaces with different areas, so the total is not a single standard formula applied twice, and reporting only the sloping side would leave out more than a third of the figure.
questions.hint: Compute the sloping side and the flat base separately, then add them.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the role of orientation in a surface integral of a vector field
questions.stem: Explain why a surface integral of a vector field cannot be evaluated until the surface has been given an orientation, and describe two conventions that fix it in common use.

answer.exemplar: The integrand of a flux integral is the field dotted with the unit normal, so the normal enters the value of the integral directly and linearly. At any smooth point a surface has exactly two unit normals, negatives of one another, and substituting one for the other changes the sign of the integrand at every point, hence the sign of the whole integral. Since a surface with no orientation has no preferred one of the pair, the integral would have two values differing only in sign and no way to choose between them, so orientation is a genuine part of the data rather than a convenience. Two conventions carry most of the work. A closed surface is oriented outward, which is well defined because the surface bounds a region and there is a definite interior to point away from. A graph of a function is usually oriented upward, meaning the normal with a positive third component, which is well defined exactly when the graph is a graph, and fails for a surface with a vertical tangent, where a different description of the surface is needed.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to name both conventions, because the answer is not that orientation matters but how a problem normally supplies it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the integrand when the normal is replaced by its negative, and then ask how a problem usually settles the choice.

measures the cone out to radius 3 instead of stopping at radius 2
forgets the tilt entirely and reports the flat annulus between the two circles

The figure 9.4248 is the flat annulus area, which omits the square root of 2 tilt factor and is the commonest way to lose it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: choose between a graph and a parametrization for a surface integral
questions.stem: Explain when it is better to describe a surface as the graph of a function and when it is better to use a two-parameter rule, and say what each description makes easy.

answer.exemplar: The graph description settles one coordinate as a function of the other two, which makes the area element a single explicit expression: the vector minus f_x, minus f_y, 1 times dx dy, with the third component fixed at 1 by the upward orientation. Everything reduces to an ordinary double integral over a region in the plane, which is the cheapest setup available whenever the surface really is a function of x and y. The price is that the description fails outright whenever the surface has a vertical tangent to the chosen projection, and it hides the answer when the region in the plane is awkward. A two-parameter rule always produces coordinates directly and handles spheres, cylinders and cones without special pleading, at the cost of having to find the tangent vectors and their cross product, and of checking that the rule is one-to-one and nondegenerate. As a working rule, use the graph when the surface is genuinely a function of the two coordinates in view, and the parametrization otherwise, especially for closed or symmetric shapes.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to give the reason for each choice, since the answer is a judgement about which obstruction each description removes.
questions.hint: Ask in each case whether the surface really is a function of the coordinates you want to project onto.
